name: Hiring and Onboarding
title: Hiring and Onboarding
answer: Hiring and onboarding is the use of AI for narrow support tasks such as drafting job postings, organizing applications, scheduling interviews, and answering routine onboarding questions from district documents. It matters because hiring decisions and the human relationships that support new staff must remain with people, while automated screening can repeat past bias and create legal exposure. The idea sets a clear boundary: AI assists, people decide.

sections.body: This idea covers where AI can help in the hiring and onboarding process and where it must stop. AI can draft job postings and check wording that might turn away qualified applicants, sort applications, and arrange interviews. It can also power an onboarding assistant that answers common questions using only district handbooks and policies. The problem it solves is administrative load and slow access to information for new staff, without handing over judgment about candidates or replacing mentors. The text is explicit that decisions about whom to interview and hire belong to people.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a district might use AI to write and review job postings, then have hiring teams review candidates themselves and treat any ranking tool only as a check. An onboarding assistant can be limited to district handbooks and policies, available at any hour, with links to official documents and a handoff to a person when it cannot answer. New teachers receive support from human mentors and colleagues, and AI can help mentors organize that support by tracking goals and scheduling check ins. Certification tracking in HR systems helps new teachers and the district keep licensing requirements in view. The text does not give grade bands for this idea, so the practice applies to district hiring and staff onboarding rather than to a specific classroom level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers one research finding on human review: when a machine ranks first, people tend to accept its choices (Krugel et al., 2023). It also states that automated screening of candidates carries serious risks, because tools that rank or filter applicants can reproduce bias from past hiring patterns and expose districts to legal claims. The text does not provide a separate evidence label, study size, or additional figures for the hiring and onboarding practices it describes. The practical guidance to have hiring teams review candidates themselves and use any tool only as a check follows from that cited finding and from the stated risks. The onboarding assistant and mentor support are presented as practice rather than as claims backed by a named study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear in the text: automated screening can reproduce bias from past hiring patterns and create legal claims, so ranking or filtering applicants is a serious risk. Decisions about whom to interview and hire stay with people, and hiring teams should review candidates themselves rather than accept a machine's order. An onboarding assistant must be limited to district handbooks and policies, link to the official documents, and hand off to a person for anything it cannot answer. Human mentors and colleagues remain the heart of onboarding, so AI should not replace those relationships. Certification tracking in HR systems supports licensing oversight, but the responsibility for meeting requirements remains with people and the district.
